changes.summary: Featuring 65 artists from more than 23 countries, this exhibition explores how abstraction emerged as a powerful visual language between 1940 and 1970, a period of global upheaval and transformation. While abstraction allowed artists across the world to move beyond realism to convey complex emotions, ideas, and experiences, it was not a singular movement. There was no one reason artists turned to abstraction, no one abstract technique or style. The impulses, methods, and resulting artworks were wildly divergent. Many artists responded to shifting social and political climates by employing materials in unexpected and, at times, deliberately destructive ways. Processes such as burning, tearing, folding, and layering embraced chance and resisted categorization. Others drew inspiration from their natural and built environments as they sought to ground themselves after the instability wrought by World War II. Some artists explored language, breaking characters and letters into illegible symbols, responding to the inability to communicate the horrors of war and through a lens of cultural exchange. As artists moved across the globe—whether through forced exile or voluntary travel for education—they formed groups to develop innovative techniques and exchange ideas. Among these groups were Gutai in Japan, Atelier 17 in Paris and New York, Tamarind Lithography Workshop in California, ZERO in Germany, and Grupo Frente in Brazil. Confronting censorship, inequality, and displacement, artists turned to abstraction as a means of practicing freedom of expression in the face of oppression and making sense of wartime atrocities.
